The statement is **TRUE**.

**Proof.**

Let $S_N(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} a_n x^n$ denote the partial sums. By hypothesis, $S_N \to f$ uniformly on $[0,1]$, so

$$\|S_N - f\|_{\infty} := \sup_{x \in [0,1]} |S_N(x) - f(x)| \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } N \to \infty.$$

Since each $S_N$ is a polynomial (hence continuous) and the convergence is uniform, $f$ is continuous on the compact set $[0,1]$, hence bounded. Since $g$ is integrable on $[0,1]$, we have $\int_0^1 |g(x)|\,dx < \infty$, and the products $S_N \cdot g$ and $f \cdot g$ are both integrable (each is the product of a bounded measurable function with an integrable function).

Now consider the difference between the two sides:

$$\left|\int_0^1 f(x)\,g(x)\,dx - \sum_{n=0}^{N} a_n \int_0^1 x^n g(x)\,dx\right| = \left|\int_0^1 \bigl(f(x) - S_N(x)\bigr)\,g(x)\,dx\right|.$$

Applying the triangle inequality and using the uniform bound on $|f - S_N|$:

$$\left|\int_0^1 \bigl(f(x) - S_N(x)\bigr)\,g(x)\,dx\right| \le \int_0^1 |f(x) - S_N(x)|\,|g(x)|\,dx \le \|f - S_N\|_{\infty} \int_0^1 |g(x)|\,dx.$$

Since $\|f - S_N\|_{\infty} \to 0$ and $\int_0^1 |g(x)|\,dx < \infty$ (a fixed finite constant), the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $N \to \infty$. Therefore

$$\sum_{n=0}^{N} a_n \int_0^1 x^n g(x)\,dx \xrightarrow{N \to \infty} \int_0^1 f(x)\,g(x)\,dx,$$

which is precisely

$$\int_0^1 f(x)\,g(x)\,dx = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n \int_0^1 x^n g(x)\,dx.$$

The interchange of the sum and the integral is justified, so term-by-term integration is valid. $\blacksquare$
